content: Opsophagos was an ancient Greek term used to describe an individual who exhibited an uncontrollable and excessive desire for fish. This term carried a deeply negative connotation, as it was not merely a critique of one’s preferences or tastes but rather an indictment of one’s moral character. To be labeled an opsophagos was to be accused of obsessive and overindulgent behavior, which was considered a serious moral failing in ancient Greek society. Such behavior was thought to signify a corruption of the soul, as proper individuals were expected to act rationally and exercise moderation in all aspects of life. Those who failed to control their desires were viewed as barbaric and uncivilized. Stories about infamous opsophagoi (the plural form of opsophagos) often depicted men who took their obsession with fish to extreme and almost unbelievable levels. These individuals were said to have trained their bodies in various ways to consume large quantities of fish immediately after it was prepared. This ensured that they could monopolize the fish for themselves, as it would still be too hot for others to touch, let alone eat. Such tales described men with heat-resistant throats and fingers padded to withstand the heat of freshly cooked fish. While these accounts were likely fictional, they served as cautionary tales, reminding listeners that succumbing to bodily pleasures at the expense of rationality and self-control was not the path to becoming an ideal human being. The message was clear: one could enjoy fish, but it was imperative to avoid taking this enjoyment to an excessive degree, lest one risk becoming an opsophagos.
